summary:
A.R.E.S. (Autonomous Route Evaluation System) is an interactive Mars EVA navigation and mission-planning platform designed to support safer and more efficient human exploration.

We developed a system combining Martian geographical data, elevation mapping, terrain classification and life-support modelling. Using a 500 × 500 grid of Jezero Crater and an eight-directional A* algorithm, A.R.E.S. calculates routes based on terrain difficulty and estimated resource consumption rather than distance alone in regard to safety.

The model considers slopes, elevation changes, walking speed, metabolic energy expenditure and temperature to estimate oxygen, water and spacesuit energy requirements. It independently optimizes outbound and return routes and assesses whether the complete excursion fits within available resource budgets.

Users can select destinations on an interactive map, explore geographical, topographical and terrain layers, evaluate mission feasibility and simulate an astronaut's journey while monitoring position, time and remaining resources.

A.R.E.S. addresses a key challenge of human Mars exploration: ensuring astronauts can reach exploration sites and return safely with limited life-support resources. By integrating navigation, terrain analysis and resource-aware planning, our system demonstrates how autonomous route optimization can support better-informed EVA decisions and future Mars missions.
details:
A.R.E.S. — Autonomous Route Evaluation System

1. What A.R.E.S. Does

A.R.E.S. (Autonomous Route Evaluation System) is an interactive Mars EVA navigation and mission-planning system designed to evaluate the feasibility of human exploration routes across the Martian surface.

The system combines planetary elevation data, terrain classification, biomechanical walking models and spacesuit resource-consumption estimates to calculate routes between a hypothetical Mars habitat and selected exploration destinations.

Unlike conventional navigation systems that prioritize geographical distance alone, A.R.E.S. evaluates the operational cost of traversing individual terrain segments. It considers how elevation changes, terrain characteristics and environmental temperature affect walking speed, energy expenditure, oxygen consumption and water requirements.

At the centre of the system is an eight-directional A* pathfinding algorithm. It calculates an optimized outbound route and independently calculates a return route, allowing the system to evaluate the complete excursion rather than assuming that the journey back will follow the same path.

The resulting mission assessment includes:

  • Outbound and return route visualization.
  • Horizontal and three-dimensional travel distance.
  • Estimated walking duration.
  • Oxygen consumption and remaining oxygen.
  • Water consumption and remaining water.
  • Spacesuit energy consumption and remaining battery capacity.
  • Elevation gain and loss.
  • Terrain composition along the route.
  • Total resource utilization compared with predefined usable budgets.
  • A round-trip feasibility assessment.

A.R.E.S. also includes an interactive EVA simulation. An astronaut marker moves along the calculated route while mission time, Martian solar time, temperature and remaining resources are updated throughout the simulated excursion.

Our objective is to demonstrate how planetary geospatial data, autonomous pathfinding and resource-aware EVA modelling can be integrated into a single mission-planning environment.

Rather than simply showing astronauts where they could travel, A.R.E.S. evaluates the estimated physical and operational demands of getting there and returning safely.

2. How It Works – Key Technical Innovations

2.1. Geospatial Data Integration and Martian Surface Representation

A.R.E.S. focuses on a localized exploration environment within Jezero Crater, Mars, using the geographical context of the Perseverance rover's exploration region.

The final navigation environment uses a 500 × 500 computational grid. Each cell represents approximately 30 × 30 metres, resulting in a geographical area of approximately 15 × 15 kilometres.

The actual midpoint of the environment is the assumed location of a theoretical Mars outpost, close to the landing site of the Perseverance rover.

The grid provides a consistent spatial structure in which elevation and terrain information can be evaluated for every potential movement.

The project uses processed planetary elevation and terrain datasets, integrated directly into the final application as embedded data matrices.

The elevation matrix is stored as floating-point values, while the terrain matrix uses integer classifications to identify the surface type associated with each cell.

The application reconstructs these matrices from compressed data when it initializes. This allows the route-planning model to operate locally within the application without having to request individual terrain values from an external service during route calculation.

The geographical representation is complemented by three selectable visualization layers:

Geographical Layer

Displays the original geographical surface map and provides the visual reference for selecting exploration destinations.

Topographical Layer

Displays the elevation representation of the selected exploration region, allowing users to identify geographical elevation variations.

Terrain Classification Layer

Displays the terrain classification matrix, showing the distribution of the surface categories used by the EVA movement model.

The user can switch between these layers while retaining the same geographical coordinate system and navigation area.

This integration allows geographical, topographical and terrain information to be considered within one unified navigation environment.

2.2. Terrain Classification and Traversability Model

A.R.E.S. distinguishes between four terrain categories in its current EVA movement model:

  1. Compact soil.
  2. Gravel.
  3. Rocky terrain.
  4. Sand.

Each terrain category is assigned individual movement parameters.

These include:

  • Relative energy expenditure.
  • Relative walking-speed factor.
  • Maximum permitted slope.
  • Sensitivity to uphill movement.

For example, compact soil is assigned a lower energy multiplier and a higher walking-speed factor than sand.

Sand is assigned a higher movement-energy multiplier, reduced walking speed and a more restrictive maximum slope.

The terrain model therefore influences how expensive and time consuming a particular movement becomes.

The system also considers elevation differences between adjacent grid cells. A movement is rejected when the resulting slope exceeds the maximum permitted slope for the terrain being entered.

This introduces a terrain dependent traversability constraint into the pathfinding process.

Rather than treating the Martian surface as a uniformly accessible grid, A.R.E.S. evaluates the physical conditions associated with individual movement segments.

2.3. Martian Biomechanical Movement Model

One of the central innovations of A.R.E.S. is its attempt to account for the physical differences between terrestrial and Martian locomotion.

The movement model incorporates Martian gravitational acceleration:

g(Mars) = 3.71 m/s²

compared with Earth's gravitational acceleration:

g(Earth) = 9.81 m/s².

The model uses the ratio between these values when estimating the metabolic cost of walking under Martian gravity.

Its metabolic movement calculation is based on a grade-dependent walking-cost relationship using the Minetti locomotion model.

The model also incorporates terrain specific energy multipliers and additional uphill movement costs.

The estimated movement speed is adjusted according to both terrain category and slope.

Consequently, two routes with identical horizontal distances can produce different estimated walking durations and resource requirements if their elevation profiles or terrain compositions differ.

This provides a more detailed representation of EVA movement than a simple constant-speed distance calculation.

The current implementation assumes an astronaut body mass of 75 kg and an additional 45 kg for the spacesuit and carried equipment.

These values are modelling assumptions used by the prototype and are not intended to represent a universal astronaut or spacesuit configuration.

2.4. Environmental Temperature Modelling

Environmental temperature is incorporated into the EVA resource model because thermal management represents an important operational requirement for spacesuit systems.

A.R.E.S. uses a Martian solar day temperature profile represented by thirteen temperature samples.

The samples are spaced at two-hour intervals, beginning at 05:10, and are interpolated to estimate temperature throughout the simulated excursion.

The user can select a departure time, allowing the model to evaluate the mission at different points in the temperature profile.

The estimated temperature influences the thermal component of the resource-consumption calculations, including heating and cooling requirements.

The simulation subsequently updates the displayed temperature as mission time progresses.

The current profile is based on values digitized from a supplied Martian temperature chart. It is therefore a representative planning profile rather than a live weather feed or a validated site-specific forecast.

2.5. Resource-Aware A* Pathfinding

The main navigation algorithm in A.R.E.S. is an eight-directional A* search implemented in JavaScript.

The algorithm operates on the 500 × 500 terrain and elevation matrices and evaluates eight possible movement directions from each grid cell.

Instead of minimizing geographical distance alone, the algorithm evaluates the estimated resource cost associated with each movement segment.

For every potential movement, the model calculates:

  • Horizontal movement distance.
  • Elevation difference.
  • Resulting slope.
  • Terrain-dependent walking speed.
  • Estimated movement duration.
  • Metabolic energy expenditure.
  • Oxygen consumption.
  • Water consumption.
  • Spacesuit energy consumption.

A movement is rejected if its slope exceeds the maximum traversable slope assigned to the terrain category.

The remaining movement cost combines the estimated consumption of oxygen, water and suit energy.

Each resource is normalized against its corresponding usable resource budget. This allows different physical quantities to contribute to a common optimization objective.

The movement cost can be represented conceptually as:

C(segment) = C(O₂) + C(H₂O) + C(Energy)

The A* algorithm accumulates these costs across the route and searches for a path with the lowest estimated total resource cost.

The heuristic uses a lower bound estimate of the minimum energy cost per metre, multiplied by the Euclidean distance remaining to the destination.

This provides an admissible lower bound estimate for guiding the search.

A binary min heap is used to manage the open nodes efficiently. The algorithm also maintains cost scores, predecessor relationships and a closed-node array.

Once the destination is reached, the predecessor relationships are reconstructed into the final path.

This approach makes resource consumption an integral part of route optimization rather than merely calculating resource use after a distance-optimized route has already been selected.

2.6. Independent Outbound and Return Route Optimization

A.R.E.S. calculates the outbound and return journeys independently.

This is an important distinction because the most suitable route from the habitat to a destination does not necessarily represent the most suitable route back.

Differences in elevation gain, descent, terrain sequence and resource expenditure can influence the optimal movement in each direction.

The application therefore performs two A* searches:

Outbound Route

Calculates the resource optimized path from the hypothetical habitat to the selected destination.

Return Route

Calculates a separate resource optimized path from the destination back to the habitat.

The interface visualizes the outbound route as a solid blue path and the return route as a dashed amber path.

The two paths can be compared geographically, while their individual resource requirements are combined to evaluate the entire excursion.

This allows the system to identify cases where a route may be feasible in one direction but exceed the available resource budget when the return journey is included.

2.7. EVA Life-Support and Resource Consumption Model

A.R.E.S. extends conventional route planning by estimating the resources required to complete an EVA.

The current model considers three principal resource categories:

Oxygen

Oxygen consumption is estimated from the calculated metabolic energy expenditure, using an energy-to-oxygen conversion factor, with an additional time dependent allowance.

The model also includes an oxygen consumption overload factor based on the estimated sustained oxygen-consumption rate.

Water

Water requirements are estimated through two components:

  • Water associated with thermal management and heat removal.
  • Water associated with estimated metabolic expenditure.

The thermal component uses a latent heat value to estimate the amount of water required for heat removal.

Spacesuit Energy

Electrical energy consumption incorporates a baseline suit power demand, temperature-dependent heating requirements and additional thermal energy requirements.

The model therefore estimates resource consumption at the level of individual movement segments rather than applying one fixed consumption rate to the entire journey.

The current nominal resource capacities are:

  • Oxygen: 1.5 kg.
  • Water: 5 kg.
  • Spacesuit energy: 2,000 Wh.

To account for operational reserves, the model only considers a portion of each nominal capacity available for planned consumption:

  • Oxygen reserve: 25%.
  • Water reserve: 20%.
  • Energy reserve: 20%.

The remaining usable budgets are therefore used when evaluating route feasibility.

These values are configurable model assumptions. They are not claimed to be official NASA spacesuit specifications or universal limits for future Mars missions.

2.8. Round-Trip Feasibility Assessment

After calculating both directions, A.R.E.S. combines their resource requirements.

For each resource, the system calculates total consumption as a proportion of the corresponding usable budget.

The round trip is classified as feasible when all three resource budgets remain within their defined limits and the route evaluation contains no blocked movement segments.

The application displays:

  • Estimated oxygen remaining at the destination.
  • Estimated water remaining at the destination.
  • Estimated suit battery remaining at the destination.
  • Total round-trip resource utilization.
  • Remaining resource-budget margin.
  • Overall feasibility status.

The minimum remaining budget margin determines the displayed operational headroom.

If all resource budgets remain within their limits, the system displays a feasible result. If any budget is exceeded, the system identifies the mission as not feasible.

This approach ensures that mission feasibility is evaluated against the complete outbound and return excursion rather than only the initial journey.

2.9. Interactive EVA Simulation and Astronaut Tracking

A.R.E.S. includes an interactive simulation that visualizes an astronaut moving along the calculated route.

Once a destination has been selected and both routes have been calculated, the user can start the simulated outbound journey.

An astronaut marker moves along the blue route, with the position updated continuously according to simulated mission progress.

When the astronaut reaches the destination, the return journey can be initiated along the independently optimized return route.

The simulation includes:

  • Forward movement.
  • Reverse movement along the return route.
  • Pause and reset controls.
  • Adjustable simulation speeds of 1×, 5×, 15× and 60×.
  • Departure-time selection.
  • Route-progress tracking.
  • Elapsed mission time.
  • Martian solar-time display.
  • Live temperature updates.
  • Remaining oxygen.
  • Remaining water.
  • Remaining suit energy.

Resource consumption is calculated progressively as the astronaut moves through individual route segments.

This means that the displayed resource levels change throughout the simulated mission rather than remaining static until the destination is reached.

The simulation provides a visual representation of how route progression, elapsed time and resource consumption are interconnected.

The positioning functionality is a software simulation based on the planned route. It does not represent live physical astronaut tracking or a deployed Martian GPS system nor the actual walking speed of an astronaut.

3. Technical Architecture and Implementation

A.R.E.S. combines a geospatial data representation with a client-side route-planning and EVA simulation model.

The final integrated application is delivered as a self-contained HTML application with its elevation and terrain matrices embedded in compressed form.

The model data is decompressed during initialization and stored in typed arrays for numerical processing.

The principal implementation technologies and methods include:

HTML and CSS

  • Application structure.
  • Interactive mission-planning interface.
  • Responsive layout and visualization panels.
  • Map-layer controls and simulation dashboard.

JavaScript

  • Terrain and elevation data loading.
  • Eight-directional A* pathfinding.
  • Resource-consumption calculations.
  • Route reconstruction.
  • Temperature interpolation.
  • EVA simulation and dynamic interface updates.

Numerical Methods

  • Euclidean distance calculations.
  • Grade-dependent movement calculations.
  • Resource normalization.
  • Linear temperature interpolation.
  • Binary min-heap priority queue.
  • Segment-by-segment resource integration.

Python and Geospatial Preprocessing

  • Raster processing.
  • Elevation and terrain extraction.
  • Geographical alignment and resampling.
  • Preparation of the matrices used by the final application.

The project also has a Python/Flask backend implementation that supports geospatial risk grid processing and route API functionality. The final integrated EVA planner uses its own embedded 500 × 500 elevation and terrain matrices and client-side resource-aware A* implementation.

Separating the data preparation process from the interactive mission planning model makes it possible to prepare planetary datasets independently and integrate the resulting matrices into the final application.

4. Representative Mission Scenario

Planning an EVA in Jezero Crater

A.R.E.S. is designed around a hypothetical Mars habitat situated within the selected Jezero Crater exploration region at around LAT: 18,43031 LON: 77,40439.

The assumed base location was calculated via "Mars Trek´s" distance and elevation measurement tools in regard to the perseverance landing site ellipse to ensure the location would be feasible as a location based on terrain, elevation and slope.

The original scientific goal inspiration was a tour from the assumed base location to the Western Delta Deposit

An astronaut begins at the habitat and selects a destination by clicking directly on the geographical map or entering geographical coordinates.

The selected destination is converted into a corresponding grid position.

The system then evaluates the elevation and terrain characteristics of the route between the habitat and the destination.

The outbound A* search calculates a resource-optimized route, while a second search calculates an independent route back to the habitat.

The resulting routes are displayed simultaneously.

The system evaluates the individual movement segments and estimates the resources required to complete each journey.

The complete mission assessment includes estimated walking duration, oxygen consumption, water consumption, battery consumption and total round-trip resource utilization.

The user can then initiate the EVA simulation to observe the astronaut progressing along the calculated route.

Throughout the simulation, the application updates the astronaut's position, elapsed time, Martian solar time, temperature and remaining resources.

This creates a complete planning sequence:

  1. Select an exploration destination.
  2. Evaluate terrain and elevation.
  3. Calculate the optimized outbound route.
  4. Calculate the optimized return route.
  5. Estimate walking time and resource consumption.
  6. Evaluate round-trip feasibility.
  7. Simulate the astronaut's excursion.

The scenario demonstrates how A.R.E.S. combines geographical navigation with resource-aware mission planning.

5. Benefits and Goals

A.R.E.S. aims to provide a more comprehensive approach to Mars EVA planning by combining geographical information with physical movement and resource constraints.

Safety first

Our main priority is the astronauts safety, therefore our risk calculation is based on the lifesupport values of the astronaut.

Resource Aware Navigation

The pathfinding algorithm optimizes estimated resource consumption instead of prioritizing geographical distance alone.

Terrain-Dependent Movement

Different terrain categories influence walking speed, energy expenditure and permitted slopes.

Elevation-Aware Planning

The system accounts for elevation changes when calculating movement costs, travel time and metabolic expenditure.

Independent Return Planning

Outbound and return journeys are optimized separately, allowing the complete excursion to be evaluated.

Integrated Life-Support Estimates

The system estimates oxygen, water and suit energy requirements for individual route segments.

Round-Trip Feasibility

Resource consumption is compared against usable budgets that account for predefined reserves.

Interactive Mission Visualization

The astronaut simulation provides a visual representation of route progression and changing mission resources.

Flexible Exploration Planning

Destinations can be selected directly through the map or by geographical coordinates, allowing users to evaluate different exploration scenarios within the selected region.

Our central goal is to demonstrate how autonomous navigation can be extended into a more complete operational planning tool, where terrain, movement, temperature and life-support resources are considered together.

6. Current Model Assumptions and Limitations

A.R.E.S. is an engineering prototype that demonstrates an integrated approach to Mars EVA route planning. Its outputs depend on the assumptions and datasets used by its underlying models.

The current implementation uses four terrain categories: compact soil, gravel, rocky terrain and sand.

The movement model uses assumed terrain parameters, a nominal astronaut mass of 75 kg and an additional 45 kg for the suit and equipment.

The resource model uses configurable nominal oxygen, water and energy capacities with predefined operational reserves.

The temperature profile is derived from a supplied chart and interpolated between its sampled values. It is not a live environmental forecast.

The resource-consumption equations are engineering estimates and have not been validated against NASA spacesuit test data or an operational Mars EVA system.

The current feasibility assessment therefore indicates whether a mission fits within the prototype's assumed resource budgets. It must not be interpreted as a certified astronaut safety determination.

The astronaut tracking feature is a route-based simulation and does not provide real-time physical positioning.

The selected terrain and elevation matrices represent a localized exploration scenario and are not a complete global representation of Mars.

These limitations define the boundaries of the current prototype while providing a clear basis for future scientific validation and development.

7. Future Development and Long-Term Vision

A.R.E.S. establishes a foundation for a more comprehensive autonomous EVA navigation and mission-support system.

Future development could focus on improving the scientific accuracy, environmental awareness and operational capabilities of the platform.

Expanded Terrain Classification

Increase the number of terrain categories and improve their physical characterization through additional scientific datasets and validation.

Improved Environmental Hazard Integration

Incorporate more detailed radiation, thermal exposure, dust and surface-hazard information into the geographical and movement models.

Dynamic Environmental Conditions

Replace representative temperature inputs with more detailed location- and time-dependent environmental datasets.

Advanced Life-Support Modelling

Improve the oxygen, water and energy models through comparison with published spacesuit specifications, human metabolic data and validated thermal-management models.

Mission Contingency Planning

Introduce additional operational scenarios, alternative destinations, emergency return planning and configurable resource reserves.

Astronaut Positioning

Develop a positioning architecture that could connect the simulated route planner to a future localized astronaut-tracking system.

Scientific Exploration Objectives

Allow mission planners to incorporate waypoints and areas of scientific interest into the route-optimization process.

Advanced Mission Interface

Continue developing the application into a comprehensive EVA planning environment with improved map visualization, mission monitoring and astronaut navigation support.


A.R.E.S. - From navigating Mars to evaluating the entire mission.
